passage:
Thursday, 9 p.m.
Today was bad. I'll write it all down.
Yesterday I borrowed Bhupen's new cycle to go to the stationery shop and hit the kerb near the temple. The front wheel bent. Pratik and Imran were with me. Pratik said, "Just park it back. He'll think it happened in the stand. Nobody will know."
All night I kept seeing Bhupen's face when his dad brought it home.
So this morning before school I told him. "I bent your wheel. It was me, not the stand. I'll pay from my savings."
He went red and shouted, "You KNEW I just got it!" He didn't talk to me all day. At lunch the cricket group sat at the other end, and Pratik said I was "stupid for telling".
It really hurt, eating alone.
But on the way home I realised I wasn't scared anymore. I didn't have to remember any story.
Chaitanya

qa.q: What did Pratik suggest doing with the cycle?
qa.a: Pratik suggested parking it back so Bhupen would think it happened in the stand.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya decide to tell Bhupen the truth?
qa.a: Chaitanya kept seeing Bhupen's face from when the cycle came home and could not live with hiding it, so guilt outweighed fear.

qa.q: Which choice cost Chaitanya most, and what did it give back?
qa.a: Owning up cost a day with Bhupen's anger and eating alone, but it gave back a feeling of not being scared and not having to remember a story.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see the honesty once his anger cools?
qa.a: Bhupen may still be upset about the wheel, but he might come to respect that Chaitanya told him directly and offered to pay.

grounding: A teenager admits to damaging Bhupen's new cycle despite peers urging a cover story, pays the price of anger and exclusion, and feels self-respect.

passage:
In the government school in Kalimpong's lower market, the chemistry practical records were due on Friday. Tanvir had got hold of last year's completed files and was passing them round the back bench.
"Just copy the readings," he told Tenzin. "Nobody does the experiments properly. Sir won't check."
Tenzin looked at the neat borrowed numbers. His own record was half empty; the lab had been closed for two weeks after it flooded.
"I'll ask sir for extra lab time," Tenzin said.
Tanvir snorted. "Fine. Be a saint. Don't expect us to wait for you at the canteen."
They didn't. For three days Tenzin ate lunch alone with his half-empty record, stomach tight. On Friday he got two extra hours in the lab with the lab assistant.
He finished late. His record was messy and his marks were average. But on the bus home, he noticed he was sitting up straight.

qa.q: Why was Tenzin's record half empty?
qa.a: The lab had been closed for two weeks after it flooded.

qa.q: What was Tenzin feeling during the three days of eating alone?
qa.a: Tenzin felt lonely and tense, stomach tight, paying the price of refusing to copy.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do instead of copying, and what did it cost and give him?
qa.a: He asked for extra lab time and did the experiments; it cost lunch company and average marks, but gave him self-respect.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see Tenzin's refusal?
qa.a: Tanvir seemed to take it as judgement, calling him a saint and leaving him out, perhaps because it made the copying feel less comfortable.

grounding: Shows a teenager refusing to copy with the group, paying with loneliness and average marks, and gaining lasting self-respect.

passage:
Two days before the regional robotics contest in Toronto, the team's robot wouldn't move. The motor smelled burnt.
"Someone must have plugged it in wrong," said Noa, the captain, looking round the school workshop. "Or it was a bad part. We'll tell Mr Kaplan it was faulty."
Bilal's stomach dropped. On Thursday night he'd stayed late and swapped two wires without checking the diagram. He was almost sure that was it.
Everyone was nodding along with "faulty part". It would be so easy.
"It was me," he said. "Thursday. I swapped the red and black on the driver board. I'm sorry."
The room went silent. Someone muttered, "Great, thanks, Bilal." Noa stared at him, jaw tight.
Mr Kaplan came in and listened. "Thank you for saying so. Now we know what to fix." They stayed till nine replacing the board.
Noa didn't talk to him on the bus. But on contest day, she handed him the screwdriver first.

qa.q: What did Bilal swap on Thursday night?
qa.a: The red and black wires on the driver board.

qa.q: What was Bilal feeling when everyone nodded along with 'faulty part'?
qa.a: Bilal's stomach dropped; he felt guilty and tempted, since staying quiet would have been so easy.

qa.q: Why did Bilal's admission help the team, despite the cost?
qa.a: Once Mr Kaplan knew the real cause, the team knew what to fix and replaced the board in time, instead of blaming a part.

qa.q: How did Noa's view of Bilal change by contest day?
qa.a: Noa was angry at first, jaw tight and silent on the bus, but by contest day showed trust by handing him the screwdriver first.

grounding: Shows a teenager admitting to his team that he caused a breakdown, risking blame, and earning back trust through honesty.

passage:
The microscope lens hit the lab floor with a small, awful click. Deepak stared at the crack running across it.

Ganga swept the glass bits into her palm. "Put it back in the box. It was already loose, okay? We all say that."

The other three nodded fast. Nobody wanted Monday detention.

Deepak put the box back on the shelf. His hands were shaking. All through the period the story sat in his stomach like a stone.

When the bell rang, he went to the lab in-charge's desk. "Sir, I dropped the microscope. It wasn't loose. It was me."

Mr Bhaskar looked at him for a long moment. "Thank you for telling me. You'll help me clean the lab after school this week."

At lunch Ganga sat at another table and didn't look up. Deepak ate alone, cheeks hot. But on the walk home, for the first time that day, he could breathe all the way in.

qa.q: What did Ganga tell the group to say about the microscope?
qa.a: Ganga said it was already loose, and they would all say that.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel while the cover story sat with him through the period?
qa.a: Deepak felt anxious and guilty; his hands were shaking and the story sat in his stomach like a stone.

qa.q: What could Deepak try tomorrow to ease things with Ganga without backing down?
qa.a: Talk to Ganga calmly, say he spoke only about his own drop and didn't want anyone in trouble, while staying clear that telling the truth was right.

qa.q: Why might Ganga react differently from Deepak?
qa.a: Ganga was probably scared of the detention and felt let down by the group plan falling apart, so she sat apart instead of seeing his choice as brave.

grounding: Shows a teenager owning up to breaking something despite a group cover story, paying with cleaning duty and a classmate's cold shoulder, and gaining lasting self-respect.
